common_name: Vaughn's Lillie Oakleaf Hydrangea (Dwarf Long-Blooming Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Vaughn's Lillie stays compact with short internodes, so it fits smaller foundation and woodland-edge beds where full-sized oakleaf cultivars would outgrow the space.

directions: Vaughn's Lillie is a compact, patented oakleaf hydrangea (U.S. Plant Patent 12,982) bred from a cross of two unnamed Hydrangea quercifolia selections, staying to just 3-4 feet tall with dense, short-jointed branching. Its rounded to conical flower panicles reach up to 5 inches long and often droop gracefully under their own weight, opening white with a faint green cast and slowly aging to soft pink over a long bloom period that runs from early summer into fall. The deeply lobed, oak-shaped leaves turn a rich burgundy-red in autumn, and mature stems develop attractive exfoliating bark for winter interest. In the Gulf South, site it where it gets morning sun and afternoon shade, since hot, humid afternoons intensify wilting on this shallow-rooted species.

common_name: Snow Giant Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large Double-Flowered Vigorous Oakleaf)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Snow Giant is a large, vigorous selection, so allow 6-8 feet in every direction at planting.

directions: Snow Giant produces some of the largest flower panicles of any oakleaf hydrangea cultivar, with fully double, densely packed sepals filling cones up to 15 inches long from early summer through mid-fall. Older florets shift toward a shell-pink overtone while newer ones near the panicle tip stay fresh white, giving each cluster a two-toned effect similar to its parent cultivar Snowflake, though Snow Giant grows noticeably larger and wider with a coarser branching habit. The bold, deeply lobed leaves color an outstanding burgundy in autumn, and the exfoliating cinnamon-brown bark exposed by leaf drop adds winter structure. Because it is one of the biggest oakleaf selections available, give it a generous woodland-edge or foundation spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in Gulf Coast gardens, where reflected heat and humidity are more intense than in its native range.

common_name: Applause Oakleaf Hydrangea (Compact Wine-Red Fall Color Oakleaf)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Applause is a smaller, more compact selection than the wild species, making it easier to fit into mixed shrub borders.

directions: Applause is a compact oakleaf hydrangea selection, noticeably smaller and denser than the species, that produces conical white flower panicles clustered at the branch tips in midsummer. Its standout feature is exceptionally deep, wine-red fall foliage color that develops even in the humid Gulf South, where oakleaf hydrangea fall color can otherwise be muted. Give it consistently moist, well-drained soil and afternoon shade in hot climates, since its smaller root mass dries out faster than larger, established oakleaf cultivars. Its reduced footprint makes it a practical choice for smaller shade gardens or foundation plantings where full-sized oakleaf cultivars would quickly become too large.

common_name: Ryan Gainey Smooth Hydrangea (Sturdy-Stemmed Native Wild Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, average to rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; cut stems back hard in late winter since flowers form on new wood.

directions: Named for Georgia garden designer Ryan Gainey, this smooth hydrangea selection produces rounded, densely packed corymbs of showy white sterile florets over a long bloom period from June into early September. Its stems are noticeably sturdier than the classic 'Annabelle', holding the flower heads upright through summer storms rather than flopping over as the blooms mature and gain weight. Because it flowers entirely on new wood, cut the whole plant back near the ground each late winter to control size and encourage a fresh flush of strong, upright growth. In Gulf Coast gardens, partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun keeps the foliage from wilting and prolongs the bloom display.

common_name: Eco Pink Puff Smooth Hydrangea (Pink-Flowered Native Wild Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, average to rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; stake or grow through supportive neighboring plants, since Eco Pink Puff's stems are notably thin and can lean under the weight of the flower clusters.

directions: Introduced by native-plant nurseryman Don Jacobs of Eco-Gardens in Decatur, Georgia, Eco Pink Puff is an unusual smooth hydrangea selection whose flower clusters are made up almost entirely of small, soft-pink fertile florets rather than the large showy sterile florets typical of most garden hydrangea cultivars. The result is a fine-textured, airy corymb that reads more like a cloud of tiny pink blossoms than a conventional lacecap or mophead, and the abundant fertile flowers make it an excellent draw for bees and other pollinators. Its stems are thinner and weaker than most arborescens cultivars, so plant it among sturdier perennials or shrubs that can lend it a little support as the flower heads fill out. Give it partial shade and reliably moist soil in the Gulf South, where its slender stems and fine foliage dry out and wilt faster than bulkier hydrangea types.

common_name: Wesser Falls Smooth Hydrangea (Wild-Collected Pink Lacecap Native Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, average to rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; site among companion plants that can help support its thin, occasionally floppy flowering stems.

directions: Wesser Falls is a wild-collected selection of smooth hydrangea, found near Wesser Falls in North Carolina's Nantahala Gorge, notable for producing soft pink-tinged lacecap flower clusters rather than the white blooms typical of the species. Its natural, unimproved habit and thin stems give it a looser, more naturalistic look than highly bred garden cultivars, making it well suited to woodland gardens and native plant plantings rather than formal borders. Historically, Wesser Falls is significant as one of the wild pink-flowered parents behind several modern pink-blooming smooth hydrangea introductions, having passed its pink coloring into the breeding lines that produced later commercial cultivars. In Gulf Coast gardens, plant it in partial shade with consistent soil moisture, since its unselected, straight-from-the-woods constitution has less heat buffering than modern compact cultivars.
